raw_case_text:
A 12-year-old Caucasian girl was diagnosed with gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease (CD), Paris classification L3, L4a, B1, G1, having presented with growth failure and abdominal pain and having undergone endoscopic and magnetic resonance enterography assessment. She failed exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) and was treated with oral prednisone tapered over 3 months with maintenance azathioprine (AZA) (2 mg/kg/day). Treatment resulted in resolution of clinical symptoms and improved biochemical markers. She had recurrence of symptoms after 9 months with abdominal pain and diarrhea. Infective work-up was negative and she was commenced on oral budesonide 9 mg and her AZA dose was increased (2.5 mg/kg/day). Thiopurine metabolites at this stage were normal [6-TGN 278 pmol/8 x 108 (normal range 230-400), 6-MMPN 734 pmol/8 x 108 (normal range <5,700)].
Three months later, she presented with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea. On examination, she was hypoxic with SaO2 90% despite 15 l/min high flow oxygen. She had severe lymphopenia (0.0 x 109/l on manual count), elevated white cell count (10.8 x 109/l), raised C-reactive protein (268 mg/l), and lactate dehydrogenase was 763 U/l. Chest X-ray showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates (Figure 1). She required intensive care for bi-level positive airway pressure respiratory support. AZA and budesonide were discontinued and she was commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam, clarithromycin, and oseltamivir to provide empiric coverage against bacteria (including atypical) and influenza, with minimal improvement in symptoms. An induced sputum sample was negative for bacterial and viral pathogens [culture and broad panel polymerase chain reaction (PCR)] but revealed P. jirovecii on silver stain (Figure 2). Intravenous (IV) trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 20 mg/kg TMP/100 mg/kg SMX and methylprednisone 1 mg/kg twice daily were initiated, which resulted in improvement in respiratory status and weaning of respiratory support over 7 days.
Prior to discharge, she was investigated for an underlying primary immunodeficiency. Human immunodeficiency (HIV) testing was negative and immunoglobulin levels were normal. B and T cell panel revealed a low absolute count of CD3, CD4, and CD8 (0.47, 0.36, 0.14 x 109/l respectively) with normal number of B cells (0.43 x 109/l), normal CD4/CD8 ratio (2.43), and a good response to previous diphtheria and tetanus vaccines. She remained lymphopenic during admission, but this slowly improved. Notably, at IBD diagnosis, she had normal lymphocyte levels [lymphocyte count 1.7-2.6 (normal range 0.9-3.5 x 109/l)]; however, after AZA initiation, she had intermittent lymphopenia (0.4-1.2 x 109/l). Thiopurine methyltransferase activity testing was unfortunately unavailable at diagnosis.
She was discharged on oral TMP-SMX for 21 days, having had 3 days of IV therapy. She received 3 days of methylprednisone followed by 5 days of oral prednisone, which was tapered over 2.5 months. AZA was restarted at a reduced dose (1.5 mg/kg/day). Within 2 months, she had normal lymphocyte numbers with a normal absolute CD4 count (0.56 x 109/l) and normal T-cell numbers. She developed an urticarial rash thought to be secondary to TMP-SMX 4 days post discharge and was changed to oral clindamycin and primaquine to complete the 21-day treatment course. She was then started on prophylactic oral dapsone, which was discontinued when she developed arthralgia. She has not subsequently taken PCP prophylaxis.
One year post-PCP admission, she was commenced on adalimumab monotherapy due to ongoing poor growth, abdominal pain, and an elevated fecal calprotectin (>1,800 mug/g). This resulted in resolution of symptoms, catch-up growth, and progression through puberty. She has had no further significant infections in the last 5 years and her lymphocyte count has remained stable.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old Caucasian girl with gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease presented with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea three months after escalating azathioprine and adding oral budesonide.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease (Paris L3, L4a, B1, G1) after presenting with growth failure and abdominal pain, the patient had initially been treated with a 3-month oral prednisone taper and maintenance azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day), during which she exhibited intermittent lymphopenia (0.4–1.2 x 10^9/L vs. pre-treatment baseline 1.7–2.6 x 10^9/L). Nine months into therapy, a clinical flare of abdominal pain and diarrhea prompted adding oral budesonide (9 mg daily) and increasing azathioprine to 2.5 mg/kg/day (with normal thiopurine metabolites: 6-TGN 278, 6-MMPN 734). Three months later, she presented with 3 days of fever, dry cough, and rapidly progressive shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gastric and ileocolonic Crohn's disease (Paris classification L3, L4a, B1, G1) with growth failure; azathioprine-induced intermittent lymphopenia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, dry cough, and severe progressive dyspnea. Subsequent post-discharge drug allergies/adverse reactions included urticarial rash to TMP-SMX and arthralgia to dapsone. Home medications on admission were azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg/day) and oral budesonide (9 mg/day).

objective.physical_examination: Severely hypoxemic on admission with SaO2 90% despite 15 L/min high-flow supplemental oxygen, requiring pediatric ICU admission for bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Profound lymphopenia with absolute manual lymphocyte count 0.0 x 10^9/L (baseline 1.7–2.6 x 10^9/L, normal: 0.9–3.5 x 10^9/L), WBC 10.8 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 268 mg/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 763 U/L. Immunological screening: HIV negative; normal serum immunoglobulin levels; preserved vaccine antibody responses to diphtheria and tetanus. Admission chest X-ray: Bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Induced sputum microbiological analysis: Negative bacterial and viral cultures and broad-panel respiratory PCR, but silver stain directly identified Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms. Pre-discharge lymphocyte subset phenotyping: Depressed absolute T-cell subsets with CD3+ 0.47 x 10^9/L, CD4+ 0.36 x 10^9/L, and CD8+ 0.14 x 10^9/L (normal CD4/CD8 ratio 2.43 and normal B-cell count 0.43 x 10^9/L; CD4+ count normalized to 0.56 x 10^9/L within 2 months).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by positive silver staining of induced sputum, LDH 763 U/L, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates) secondary to azathioprine- and budesonide-induced profound T-cell lymphopenia (manual lymphocyte count 0.0 x 10^9/L) in a 12-year-old girl with Crohn's disease. Plan and clinical course: Azathioprine and budesonide were stopped, BiPAP support was instituted in the PICU, and after minimal response to empiric piperacillin-tazobactam, clarithromycin, and oseltamivir, targeted intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX 20 mg/kg TMP / 100 mg/kg SMX) plus IV methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days, then oral prednisone tapered over 2.5 months) were initiated, weaning her off respiratory support over 7 days. Four days after discharge on oral TMP-SMX, an urticarial drug rash prompted switching to oral clindamycin plus primaquine to complete the 21-day course (and subsequent prophylactic dapsone was stopped due to arthralgia). One year later, she was transitioned to adalimumab monotherapy with sustained remission, catch-up growth, and stable lymphocyte counts over 5 years of follow-up.
